title: Chemical equilibrium, pH & buffers
outcomes: Chemical equilibrium and the equilibrium constant

summary.overview: Every reaction tends towards an equilibrium described by Keq. Water itself ionises slightly, which sets up the pH scale. Weak acids are characterised by their pKa, and mixtures of a weak acid and its conjugate base (buffers) keep the pH of cells and blood within narrow limits.

sections.heading: Equilibrium
points: At equilibrium, Keq = [products] / [reactants], each raised to its stoichiometric power.
A large Keq means products are favoured. Keq is fixed at a given temperature, whatever the starting concentrations.
Catalysts, including enzymes, reach equilibrium faster but never change Keq.

sections.heading: Ionisation of water and pH
points: H2O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻. Because [H2O] is constant (55.5 M), Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ M² at 25 °C.
In pure water, [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ M, so pH = 7.
The scale is logarithmic: 1 pH unit = a 10-fold change in [H⁺].

sections.heading: Weak acids, Ka and pKa
points: Weak acids dissociate only partly: HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, with Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA].
pKa = −log Ka; the lower the pKa, the stronger the acid.
Example: 0.1 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵) gives [H⁺] ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ M, so pH ≈ 2.88.
If x ≪ [HA], the approximation [HA] ≈ starting concentration avoids solving a quadratic.

sections.heading: Buffers and Henderson–Hasselbalch
points: A buffer is a weak acid plus its conjugate base; it resists changes in pH.
At pH = pKa the acid and base forms are 50:50, and buffering capacity is greatest.
Buffering is lost once the pH is more than about 1 unit away from the pKa.

sections.heading: Biological buffers
points: Phosphate (H2PO4⁻/HPO4²⁻, pKa ≈ 6.86) buffers the cytoplasm at millimolar levels.
Bicarbonate (CO2/HCO3⁻, pKa ≈ 6.1) is the key blood-plasma buffer. Because CO2 is exhaled and HCO3⁻ is regulated by the kidney, it works well at pH 7.4.
Histidine's imidazole (pKa ≈ 6) lets proteins buffer near neutral pH.
Laboratory buffers such as HEPES, PIPES and CHES are sulphonic acids of cyclic amines, chosen for pKa values near physiological pH.

keyTerms.definition: Ratio of product to reactant concentrations at equilibrium.
Ion product of water: [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ M² at 25 °C.
−log Ka; the pH at which an acid is half dissociated.
Weak acid and conjugate base mixture that resists pH change.

examTips: pH = pKa means [A⁻] = [HA]: buffering is strongest there.
Each extra pH unit above the pKa multiplies [A⁻]/[HA] by 10.
Lower pKa = stronger acid = more dissociated at a given pH.
Remember pH + pOH = 14, and that [H⁺] at pH 3 is 100× that at pH 5.

questions.outcome: Chemical equilibrium and the equilibrium constant
questions.stem: For the reaction A ⇌ B, K′eq = 1000. What does this tell you?

options.text: At equilibrium [B] is 1000 times [A], so the reaction strongly favours B
options.why: Keq = [B]/[A] at equilibrium; a large value means products dominate.

options.text: The reaction reaches equilibrium very quickly, within a fraction of a second
options.why: Keq says nothing about rate; that depends on ΔG‡.

options.text: Adding an enzyme would shift the equilibrium further and raise K′eq above 1000
options.why: Catalysts never change Keq.

options.text: The reaction cannot run in reverse, because B does not convert back into A
options.why: The reverse reaction still occurs; at equilibrium the two rates are equal.

questions.stem: What is the ion product of water (Kw) at 25 °C?

options.why: 10⁻⁷ M is each ion's concentration in pure water, not their product.
That ratio is 1 only in a neutral solution; Kw is a product.
This is the molarity of pure water, used to derive Kw.

questions.stem: Gastric juice has [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻² M. What are its pH and [OH⁻]?

options.why: That describes a strongly basic solution; this is the pOH confused with the pH.
[H⁺] and [OH⁻] must multiply to 10⁻¹⁴ M².
The sign is wrong: pH = −log[H⁺] = +2.

questions.stem: How many times higher is [H⁺] in urine at pH 5 than in blood at pH 7?

options.text: 100 times
options.why: Two pH units = 10² = 100-fold, because the scale is logarithmic.

options.text: 2 times
options.why: pH is not linear; each unit is a factor of 10.

options.text: 20 times
options.why: Two units means 10 × 10 = 100, not 10 × 2.

options.text: 1000 times
options.why: A 1000-fold difference needs 3 pH units.

questions.stem: A cleaning solution has pOH = 4. What is its pH?

options.why: pH + pOH = 14, so pH = 14 − 4 = 10 (basic).
This is the pOH, not the pH.
pH and pOH are subtracted from 14, not added to it.
pH 7 would need pOH 7.

questions.stem: 0.1 mol of acetic acid (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ M) is dissolved in water to make 1 L. Assuming the acid is the only source of H⁺, what is the approximate pH?

options.why: That assumes complete dissociation, which is true only of a strong acid.
4.76 is the pKa, the pH of an equimolar acetic acid/acetate buffer.
That would need a 10:1 acetate-to-acid ratio.

questions.stem: In the acetic acid calculation, why may we approximate [HA] ≈ 0.1 M instead of (0.1 − x)?

options.text: Only about 1.3% of the acid dissociates, so x is negligible next to 0.1 M
options.why: For sufficiently weak acids x ≪ [HA]; check afterwards that this holds.

options.text: Acetic acid does not dissociate at all, so its concentration stays exactly 0.1 M
options.why: It dissociates slightly; otherwise the pH would be 7.

options.text: Water contributes most of the H⁺ in the solution, so the acid's own x does not matter
options.why: The calculation assumes the acid is the only significant H⁺ source.

options.text: The approximation works equally well for strong acids at 0.1 M, such as HCl
options.why: Strong acids dissociate completely, so x is not small.

questions.stem: Lactic acid has pKa ≈ 3.9 and acetic acid pKa ≈ 4.8. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Lactic acid is the stronger acid and is more dissociated at any given pH
options.why: A lower pKa means a larger Ka, so the acid gives up H⁺ more readily.

options.text: Acetic acid is the stronger acid, because a higher pKa means it releases more H⁺
options.why: A higher pKa means a weaker acid.

options.text: Both acids are fully dissociated at pH 3, because pH 3 is below both of their pKa values
options.why: At pH 3, below both pKa values, the protonated (HA) forms dominate.

options.text: pKa has no relation to acid strength; only the concentration of the acid matters
options.why: pKa is the standard measure of acid strength.

questions.stem: An acetate buffer (pKa 4.76) contains 10 times more acetate than acetic acid. What is its pH?

options.why: This would be the pH with 10 times more acid than base.
pH = pKa only when [A⁻] = [HA].
The log of the ratio (1) is added, not the ratio itself.

questions.stem: The H2PO4⁻/HPO4²⁻ pair has pKa ≈ 6.86. At pH 6.86, what fraction of this phosphate is present as HPO4²⁻?

options.why: At pH = pKa, log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 0, so the two forms are equal.
10% HPO4²⁻ would occur about 1 pH unit below the pKa.
90% would occur about 1 pH unit above the pKa.
A buffer at its pKa contains both forms.

questions.stem: Why is an acetate buffer (pKa 4.76) a poor choice for an experiment run at pH 7.4?

options.text: At pH 7.4, over 2 units above the pKa, nearly all is acetate, leaving little acid to neutralise base
options.why: Buffering capacity is lost once pH is more than about 1 unit from the pKa.

options.text: Acetate is toxic to all enzymes at pH 7.4, so it would stop the reaction being studied completely
options.why: The problem is buffering capacity, not toxicity.

options.text: Acetate buffers only work above pH 10, where the acetic acid is fully protonated and ready to react
options.why: Acetate buffers best around pH 3.8–5.8.

options.text: The buffer would hold the pH at exactly 4.76, because a buffer always fixes the pH at its own pKa
options.why: A buffer's pH depends on the [A⁻]/[HA] ratio; the problem is weak resistance to change.

questions.stem: Blood pH is 7.4 and the effective pKa of the CO2/HCO3⁻ system is 6.1. What is the ratio [HCO3⁻] : [dissolved CO2] in normal blood?

options.text: About 20 : 1
About 1 : 1
options.why: A 1:1 ratio would mean pH = 6.1.

options.text: About 1 : 20
options.why: This inverts the ratio; pH is above the pKa, so the base form dominates.

options.text: About 1.3 : 1
options.why: 1.3 is the log of the ratio, not the ratio itself.

questions.stem: A calf with severe diarrhoea loses large amounts of bicarbonate in its faeces, while its blood pCO2 stays roughly constant. What happens to blood pH, and why?

options.text: It falls (metabolic acidosis), because [HCO3⁻]/[CO2] drops in pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3⁻]/[CO2])
options.why: Losing base lowers the ratio, so the pH drops below 7.4.

options.text: It rises (alkalosis), because bicarbonate is an acid and losing it leaves fewer H⁺ in the blood
options.why: HCO3⁻ is the base form; losing it acidifies the blood.

options.text: It stays at exactly 7.4, because the blood buffers hold the pH constant whatever is lost
options.why: Buffers resist pH change but cannot stop it when the buffer itself is lost.

options.text: It falls, because CO2 is exhaled faster and the lungs remove the blood's main base
options.why: The question states that pCO2 is unchanged; faster exhalation would raise pH.

questions.stem: Why do histidine residues help proteins act as buffers near neutral pH?

options.text: The imidazole side chain has a pKa of about 6, close to physiological pH, so it takes up or releases H⁺
options.why: Groups buffer best within about 1 unit of their pKa.

options.text: Histidine's side-chain carboxyl group has a pKa of about 12, so it releases H⁺ when the pH starts to rise
options.why: α-Carboxyl groups have pKa ≈ 2.

options.text: Histidine is negatively charged at physiological pH, so it binds any H⁺ that is added to the cell
options.why: Its imidazole is neutral or positive depending on pH.

options.text: Histidine forms stable covalent bonds with H⁺, removing the protons from solution permanently
options.why: Protonation is a reversible acid–base reaction.

questions.stem: Which buffer system is most important in mammalian blood plasma?

options.text: Bicarbonate (CO2/HCO3⁻)
options.why: CO2 is exhaled by the lungs and HCO3⁻ is regulated by the kidneys, so the system can be adjusted.

options.text: HEPES (a Good's buffer)
options.why: HEPES is a synthetic buffer used in the laboratory (in vitro).

options.text: Acetate (acetic acid)
options.why: Acetate's pKa (4.76) is far from blood pH.

options.text: Hydrochloric acid (HCl)
options.why: HCl is a strong acid, not a buffer.

flashcards.back: [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ M². In pure water each ion is 10⁻⁷ M.

flashcards.front: Definition of pH; link to pOH?
flashcards.back: pH = −log[H⁺]; pH + pOH = 14. 1 unit = 10-fold change in [H⁺].

flashcards.outcome: Chemical equilibrium and the equilibrium constant
flashcards.back: Only temperature. Neither starting concentrations nor catalysts change it.
Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]; pKa = −log Ka. Lower pKa = stronger acid.

flashcards.front: Shortcut for [H⁺] of a weak acid?
When is buffering capacity greatest? When is it lost?
flashcards.back: Greatest at pH = pKa (50:50). Lost beyond about ±1 pH unit from the pKa.
Phosphate (intracellular, pKa ≈ 6.86), bicarbonate (blood plasma, pKa ≈ 6.1), histidine side chains (proteins, pKa ≈ 6).
HEPES, PIPES, CHES: sulphonic acids of cyclic amines with pKa values near physiological pH.
